title: Included columns and covering indexes
description: Learn how to use included columns to create covering indexes that eliminate expensive key lookups.

data.text: In SQL Server, an index key is used to search and sort the B-tree. Included columns are stored at the leaf level only and do not participate in the key structure. By adding non-key columns to an index, you can create a covering index that satisfies a query without touching the base table.

When SQL Server uses a nonclustered index but the index does not contain all the columns needed by the query, it performs a key lookup (also called a bookmark lookup) back to the clustered index or heap for each matching row. For queries that return many rows, these lookups can dominate the total cost.

data.title: Query that causes a key lookup
data.content: This query selects CustomerName and TotalAmount filtered by OrderDate. An index on OrderDate alone is not enough.
data.code:
SELECT
    CustomerName,
    TotalAmount
FROM dbo.Orders
WHERE OrderDate >= '2024-01-01';

data.title: Create a covering index
data.content: Include the extra columns so the query can be satisfied entirely from the index. No lookup to the clustered index is needed.

data.title: Differences to remember
items: Key columns are stored at every level of the B-tree and determine sort order
Included columns are stored at the leaf level only
Included columns do not affect the index key size
You can include up to 1,023 included columns per index

data.title: Index width is a balancing act
data.text: Key columns increase the size of every page in the index. Included columns increase only the leaf pages. Use included columns for wider payloads that are needed for output but not for searching or grouping.

data.title: Verify a covering index with an execution plan
data.content: After creating the covering index, check that the Key Lookup operator has disappeared from the plan.

data.title: Takeaway
points: Included columns add data to the leaf level without changing the key structure
Covering indexes remove the need for expensive key lookups
Use included columns for columns needed in SELECT but not in WHERE or JOIN
Keep the key as narrow as possible and push wide columns to INCLUDE
data.takeaway: Covering indexes are one of the simplest and most effective ways to reduce query cost in SQL Server.
